note: The counted exception to fill-empty-only: every theme here exists in the source with a band-suffixed description (the documented content debt); this promotion replaces exactly those rows with five authored sentences per theme. The normaliser refuses any other target. Track names, prefixes, codes, credentials and transfer checks are untouched.

themes.description: The difference between a question that is interesting and one that has a possible answer.

bands.K–2: Ask a 'why' question about something in the room and, with an adult, turn it into one you could test today.
bands.3–5: Take one big question from class and write two smaller ones you could actually answer with what is in the school.
bands.6–8: Take a vague question and produce three answerable versions of it, and have a teacher say which one a class could test.
bands.9–10: Take a vague question and produce three answerable versions of it.
bands.11–12: Take a real research question from a lab, department or partner, produce three answerable versions, and get one adopted for a real study.

themes.description: Reading structure first, methods second, abstract last, and where the real claim sits.

bands.K–2: Look at a science book page with an adult: find the picture, the big claim, and one thing that shows it is true.
bands.3–5: Read a short science article and write the claim and the evidence on two separate lines.
bands.6–8: Read one short paper structure first, methods second, abstract last, and summarise the claim and the evidence separately for a checker.
bands.9–10: Read one paper this way and summarise the claim and the evidence separately.
bands.11–12: Read three papers this way for a real journal club or lab meeting, and present where each claim exceeds its evidence.

themes.description: Finding what has been tried, including the attempts that were never published.

bands.K–2: Before doing an experiment, ask two people whether they have tried it and what happened.
bands.3–5: Find out what a classmate or a book already tried on your question before you start, and write it down.
bands.6–8: Produce a prior-work summary for a school project that includes at least one attempt that did not work, with a teacher checking sources.
bands.9–10: Produce a prior-work summary that includes at least one unpublished or null result.
bands.11–12: Produce a prior-work summary for a real study that includes unpublished or null results, and have a specialist confirm nothing major is missing.

themes.theme: Framing a hypothesis you could be wrong about
themes.description: Framing so that a result could contradict you, which is the whole point of the exercise.

bands.K–2: Say what you think will happen in a class experiment, and what you would see if you were wrong.
bands.3–5: Write a prediction for a school experiment and the result that would prove it wrong.
bands.6–8: State a hypothesis for a real school experiment and the exact observation that would falsify it, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: State your hypothesis and the observation that would falsify it.
bands.11–12: State the hypothesis and the falsifying observation for a real study, in writing, before data is collected, and have a colleague sign it.

themes.theme: Scope: the study you can actually run
themes.description: Scoping to the study you can actually run with the time, money and access you have.

bands.K–2: Plan an experiment you could finish in one lesson with what is in the classroom.
bands.3–5: Cut a big project idea down to what you can do in a week with school materials, and say what you left out.
bands.6–8: Cut a proposed school study to what the real time, materials and access permit, and name what you lost, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Cut a proposed study to what your real constraints permit, and name what you lost.
bands.11–12: Cut a real proposed study to its real constraints with the people who hold the budget and the access, and document what was lost and why.

themes.description: Committing to the analysis before seeing the data, and why that feels like a cost.

bands.K–2: Before an experiment, tell an adult exactly how you will decide who won, and stick to it.
bands.3–5: Write down before a school experiment how you will measure the result, and do not change it afterwards.
bands.6–8: Write a preregistration for a small school study, including how the data will be analysed, and lodge it with a teacher before collecting anything.
bands.9–10: Write a preregistration for a small study, including the analysis plan.
bands.11–12: Write and lodge a preregistration for a real study on a public registry or with a real supervisor, including the analysis plan.

themes.theme: Talking to somebody who disagrees early
themes.description: Finding disagreement early, when it is cheap, rather than at review, when it is not.

bands.K–2: Tell a friend your experiment idea and listen to one reason it might not work.
bands.3–5: Present a project idea to a classmate who might disagree, and write down their objection.
bands.6–8: Present a real project question to somebody likely to object, record the objection, and say what you changed.
bands.9–10: Present your question to somebody likely to object and record their objection.
bands.11–12: Present a real study question to a critical specialist before design is fixed, and document the objections and the design changes they caused.

themes.description: The literature that undercuts your idea is the most valuable literature you will read.

bands.K–2: Find one thing in a book that says the opposite of what you thought, and tell an adult.
bands.3–5: Find one source that disagrees with your class project idea and say why it might be right.
bands.6–8: Find the strongest contrary source for a school project and state what it would take to reconcile the two, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Find the strongest contrary paper and state what it would take to reconcile.
bands.11–12: Find the strongest contrary paper to a real study, reconcile or concede in writing, and present the result to the team.

themes.description: Stopping before you start, and why that decision is almost never rewarded.

bands.K–2: Say why you might decide not to do an experiment, and what would change your mind.
bands.3–5: Write the case for not doing one school project, and what would make it worth doing.
bands.6–8: Write the case for not running one proposed school study, and the conditions that would change it, for a teacher to judge.
bands.9–10: Write the case for not running one study, and the conditions that would change it.
bands.11–12: Write the case for not running a real proposed study, present it to the people who wanted it, and record the decision.

themes.theme: Writing the question down before the method
themes.description: Writing the question first fixes the method to the question rather than the reverse.

bands.K–2: Say your question out loud before choosing what to do, and have an adult write it down.
bands.3–5: Write your question on one page before deciding how to answer it, and date it.
bands.6–8: Produce a one-page question document for a school study, dated before any method is chosen, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Produce a one-page question document dated before any method is chosen.
bands.11–12: Produce a dated question document for a real study and show, at the end, where the method served the question and where it did not.

themes.description: Selecting an instrument for the measurement you need, not the one already on the bench.

bands.K–2: Pick the right measuring tool for a class job — ruler, scale or cup — and say why.
bands.3–5: Choose a measuring instrument for a school experiment and say why it is precise enough.
bands.6–8: Justify an instrument choice for a real school experiment against the precision the question requires, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Justify an instrument choice against the precision the question requires.
bands.11–12: Justify an instrument choice for a real study in writing, against the precision required and the alternatives available, for a supervisor to approve.

themes.theme: Calibration and the drift you did not see
themes.description: Calibration as a schedule rather than an event, and the drift that hides between them.

bands.K–2: Check a scale reads zero with nothing on it before weighing, and tell an adult if it does not.
bands.3–5: Check a measuring instrument against something known before a school experiment, and write what you found.
bands.6–8: Produce a calibration record for a school instrument over several sessions and identify the drift it would have caught.
bands.9–10: Produce a calibration record and identify the drift it would have caught.
bands.11–12: Set up and keep a calibration schedule for a real instrument, and show the drift the schedule caught that an event would have missed.

themes.theme: Controls, and what each one rules out
themes.description: Every control rules out one specific alternative explanation. Naming which.

bands.K–2: In a class experiment, say what the 'nothing changed' cup is for.
bands.3–5: For a school experiment, name the control and say what it rules out.
bands.6–8: For a real school protocol, state what each control eliminates, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: For a real protocol, state what each control eliminates.
bands.11–12: For a real study protocol, state what each control eliminates and add the control the protocol was missing.

themes.description: Deciding how many before collecting any, and what happens when you decide after.

bands.K–2: Say how many times you would repeat a test before believing the answer, and why.
bands.3–5: Decide how many measurements a school experiment needs before starting, and explain why that number.
bands.6–8: Perform a simple sample-size calculation for a school study and state its assumptions, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Perform a sample size calculation and state its assumptions.
bands.11–12: Perform and document a sample-size calculation for a real study, state the assumptions, and have them challenged by a statistician or supervisor.

themes.description: Blinding where the design permits it, and being explicit where it does not.

bands.K–2: Do a taste or sound test where the person guessing cannot see the answer, and say why that matters.
bands.3–5: Design a school experiment where the person judging does not know which is which.
bands.6–8: Identify where blinding is possible in a real school study and where it is not, with reasons, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Identify where blinding is possible in your work and where it is not, with reasons.
bands.11–12: Identify blinding for a real study in its protocol, with reasons where it is impossible, and have the protocol reviewed.

themes.theme: Recording what you did as you do it
themes.description: Recording contemporaneously, because reconstructed records are a different kind of record.

bands.K–2: Write or draw each step of an experiment as you do it, not afterwards.
bands.3–5: Keep a log of a school experiment as it happens, with times.
bands.6–8: Keep a contemporaneous log for one full school procedure and have a teacher compare it with what they saw.
bands.9–10: Keep a contemporaneous log for one full procedure.
bands.11–12: Keep contemporaneous records for a real procedure to a standard an audit would accept, and have them audited.

themes.theme: The protocol deviation and logging it
themes.description: A deviation from protocol is data about the study; hiding it is data about you.

bands.K–2: When you do a step differently from the plan, tell an adult and write it down.
bands.3–5: When a school experiment goes off plan, write what changed and why.
bands.6–8: Log a real deviation in a school experiment with its cause and its likely effect on the result.
bands.9–10: Log a real deviation with its cause and its likely effect.
bands.11–12: Log real deviations for a study and present them with the results so a reader can weigh them.

themes.description: Distinguishing contamination, instrument error and a genuine negative result.

bands.K–2: When an experiment gives a strange answer, say whether the tool, the mess, or the idea was the reason.
bands.3–5: Take one odd result from a school experiment and say whether it was contamination, instrument error, or real.
bands.6–8: Take three anomalous results from school experiments and classify each with the evidence, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Take three anomalous results and classify each with the evidence.
bands.11–12: Take three anomalous results from a real study, classify each with the evidence, and record the decision in the study's record.

themes.theme: A method somebody else could repeat
themes.description: Writing a method somebody else could execute without asking you a question.

bands.K–2: Write an experiment's steps so a classmate can do it without asking you anything.
bands.3–5: Give your written method to a classmate and count the questions they had to ask.
bands.6–8: Hand your method to somebody who has not seen it and record every question they ask, then fix the method.
bands.9–10: Hand your method to somebody who has not seen it and record every question they ask.
bands.11–12: Hand a real method to an outside person, record every question, and publish the corrected method with the study.

themes.theme: When the method decides the answer
themes.description: When the method constrains the answer, and how to notice that before publication.

bands.K–2: Say how measuring in a different way could change the answer of a class experiment.
bands.3–5: Find one choice in a school experiment that limits what you could find out.
bands.6–8: Identify one methodological choice in a real school study that bounds what could be concluded, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Identify one methodological choice in your work that bounds what you could conclude.
bands.11–12: Identify the method-bound conclusions in a real study and write them into its limitations before publication.

themes.description: Raw data is never edited. Everything else is a derived copy with a recorded transformation.

bands.K–2: Keep your first measurements on their own page and never rub them out; copy them to work on.
bands.3–5: Keep the original data sheet of a school experiment untouched and work only on a copy.
bands.6–8: Produce a folder structure for a school project that makes overwriting the raw data difficult, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Produce a directory structure that makes overwriting raw data difficult.
bands.11–12: Set up and enforce a raw-data policy for a real project, with the structure and permissions that make overwriting impossible.

themes.theme: Version control for things that are not code
themes.description: Versioning notebooks, protocols, spreadsheets and images, not only code.

bands.K–2: Save your experiment sheet with a new name each time you change it, so the old one is still there.
bands.3–5: Keep numbered versions of a school project document and say what changed in each.
bands.6–8: Set up and demonstrate versioning for one non-code artefact — a protocol, a spreadsheet, an image — in a school project.
bands.9–10: Set up and demonstrate versioning for one non-code artefact.
bands.11–12: Set up versioning for every non-code artefact of a real project and show a colleague how to recover any version.

themes.theme: Missing data and what you do about it
themes.description: Missingness is information. Recording why a value is absent before deciding what to do.

bands.K–2: When a measurement is missing, write why it is missing instead of making one up.
bands.3–5: Mark every missing value in a school dataset with the reason it is missing.
bands.6–8: Classify the missing values in one school dataset by cause, and say what you did about each, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Classify the missing values in one dataset by cause.
bands.11–12: Classify missingness in a real dataset by cause, choose and justify the handling for each, and document it in the analysis record.

themes.description: An outlier is a hypothesis about an error until you have investigated it.

bands.K–2: When one measurement looks wrong, check it again before crossing it out.
bands.3–5: Find one odd number in a school dataset, investigate it, and say whether to keep it.
bands.6–8: Investigate one outlier in a school dataset and document the decision to keep or exclude it, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Investigate one outlier and document the decision to keep or exclude.
bands.11–12: Investigate every outlier in a real dataset, document each decision, and show the analysis both with and without them.

themes.theme: Statistics you understand versus statistics you cite
themes.description: Using the test you can explain, and citing nothing you could not derive the meaning of.

bands.K–2: Explain what an average is using a handful of measurements, in your own words.
bands.3–5: Explain one way of summarising data — average, range or median — in writing, without jargon.
bands.6–8: Explain one statistical test used in a school project, in writing, without jargon, to a classmate who then explains it back.
bands.9–10: Explain one statistical test you use, in writing, without jargon.
bands.11–12: Explain every statistical test in a real analysis in writing without jargon, and remove any you cannot.

themes.theme: P-values and what they do not mean
themes.description: What a p-value is, what it is not, and the four claims routinely made that it cannot support.

bands.K–2: Say what it means when a result could have happened by chance.
bands.3–5: Explain, with a coin-flip example, why a surprising result can still be chance.
bands.6–8: Correct two misstatements about p-values from real published text, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Correct four misstatements about p-values from real published text.
bands.11–12: Correct four misstatements about p-values in real published text and write the correct sentence for each, for a real audience.

themes.theme: Plotting the data before modelling it
themes.description: Looking at the data before modelling it, because the plot finds what the model assumes away.

bands.K–2: Draw a picture of your measurements before saying what they show.
bands.3–5: Plot a school dataset before working out any summary, and say what the plot shows.
bands.6–8: Produce the diagnostic plots for one school dataset before any model is fitted, and say what they rule out.
bands.9–10: Produce the diagnostic plots for one dataset before any model is fitted.
bands.11–12: Produce and archive the diagnostic plots for a real dataset before modelling, and show what the plots found that the model would have assumed away.

themes.theme: Sharing data somebody else can use
themes.description: A dataset somebody else can use has a dictionary, units, provenance and a licence.

bands.K–2: Label your measurements with what they are and what unit they are in so a friend can read them.
bands.3–5: Share a school dataset with a heading for every column and the units written in.
bands.6–8: Publish one small school dataset with a dictionary, units, provenance and a licence, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Publish one small dataset with all four present.
bands.11–12: Publish a real dataset with all four present to a repository, and have an outside person use it without asking a question.

themes.description: Consent for human data, what it covered, and the analysis it does not permit.

bands.K–2: Ask a classmate before writing down anything about them, and say what you will use it for.
bands.3–5: Write a consent note for a class survey saying what is collected and what it is for.
bands.6–8: Read one consent form and state an analysis it would not authorise, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Read one consent form and state an analysis it would not authorise.
bands.11–12: Review the consent for a real dataset, state what it does and does not authorise, and stop one analysis it would not.

themes.description: Nothing is deleted quietly. Removal is recorded with a reason and a name.

bands.K–2: If you remove a measurement, write why and put your name next to it.
bands.3–5: Keep a list of anything removed from a school dataset, with the reason and who removed it.
bands.6–8: Demonstrate a deletion log for one real removal in a school project.
bands.9–10: Demonstrate a deletion log for one real removal.
bands.11–12: Keep a deletion log for a real project and have it audited against the raw data.

themes.description: Somebody replicating your work is treating it as important. Responding accordingly.

bands.K–2: Let a classmate repeat your experiment and be glad if they get the same answer.
bands.3–5: Give a classmate everything they need to repeat your school experiment, before they ask.
bands.6–8: Prepare the package a replicator would need for a school study, before anyone asks, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Prepare the package a replicator would need, before anyone asks.
bands.11–12: Prepare and publish the replication package for a real study, and respond to a real replication attempt on the record.

themes.theme: Your own results, one year later
themes.description: Attempting your own result a year later, which is the cheapest reproducibility test there is.

bands.K–2: Repeat an experiment you did last term using only your old notes, and see if it matches.
bands.3–5: Redo a school experiment from last year from your own records alone.
bands.6–8: Reproduce one of your own school results from your own records alone, and record what was missing from them.
bands.9–10: Reproduce one of your own results from your own records alone.
bands.11–12: Reproduce a real result of your own from records alone a year on, and report the outcome to the team either way.

themes.theme: A lab notebook a stranger could follow
themes.description: A notebook written for a stranger, because in two years you are the stranger.

bands.K–2: Write your experiment notes so someone who was not there could follow them.
bands.3–5: Have a classmate follow one page of your science notebook and say where they got lost.
bands.6–8: Have somebody unfamiliar follow one of your notebook entries and fix what they could not follow.
bands.9–10: Have somebody unfamiliar follow one of your notebook entries.
bands.11–12: Have an outside person follow a real notebook entry for a real procedure, and adopt the notebook standard that follows.

themes.description: Capturing the environment as well as the code, since versions decide results.

bands.K–2: Write down which app or tool you used so someone else can use the same one.
bands.3–5: Record the exact tools and versions used for a school data project.
bands.6–8: Produce a runnable environment specification for one school analysis, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Produce a runnable environment specification for one analysis.
bands.11–12: Produce an environment specification for a real analysis and have it run by somebody else on a different machine.

themes.theme: The result that will not reproduce
themes.description: The result that will not reproduce, and the interval before you know which of you is wrong.

bands.K–2: When a friend gets a different answer, work out together who was right without falling out.
bands.3–5: When a school experiment cannot be repeated, write what each side did differently.
bands.6–8: Document a failed reproduction of a school result fairly, from both sides, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Document a failed reproduction fairly, from both sides.
bands.11–12: Document a real failed reproduction fairly from both sides, and publish or share it with the original authors.

themes.description: Publishing a null result, where to publish it, and why it matters to people you will never meet.

bands.K–2: Tell the class when an experiment did not work, and what you learned from it.
bands.3–5: Write up a school experiment that found nothing, as carefully as one that did.
bands.6–8: Draft a null-result write-up for a school study to the same standard as a positive one.
bands.9–10: Draft a null result write-up to publication standard.
bands.11–12: Write up a real null result to publication standard and submit it where null results are published.

themes.description: Correcting the record: the mechanisms, their speed, and the reputational arithmetic.

bands.K–2: When you made a mistake in a class chart, fix it and tell everyone what changed.
bands.3–5: Write a correction note for a school report that had an error, saying what was wrong.
bands.6–8: Draft a correction for a real or worked error in a school report, following what a journal would need.
bands.9–10: Draft a correction for a real or worked error.
bands.11–12: Issue a real correction through the real mechanism, and record how long it took and what it cost.

themes.description: Preprints, peer review, and what each one does and does not certify.

bands.K–2: Say the difference between showing a friend your work and having a teacher check it.
bands.3–5: Explain what it means for other scientists to check a paper before it is published.
bands.6–8: Explain to a non-specialist what peer review does and does not guarantee, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Explain to a non-specialist what peer review does and does not guarantee.
bands.11–12: Explain peer review and preprints to a real non-specialist audience and answer their questions accurately.

themes.theme: Fraud, error and the space between
themes.description: Fraud, error, and the large space between them where most problems actually live.

bands.K–2: Say the difference between a mistake and cheating in a class experiment.
bands.3–5: Sort three cases of wrong results into mistake, carelessness, or cheating, and say why.
bands.6–8: Classify three documented cases and defend each classification, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Classify three documented cases and defend each classification.
bands.11–12: Classify three documented cases for a real training session, defend each, and state the institutional response each warranted.

themes.theme: What reproducibility costs and who pays
themes.description: Reproducibility has a cost, it falls on somebody, and pretending otherwise is why it does not happen.

bands.K–2: Say what it would take to redo a class experiment, and who would have to give the time.
bands.3–5: Work out how long it would take to repeat a school project, and who would pay for that time.
bands.6–8: Cost the reproducibility work for one school project and identify who pays, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Cost the reproducibility work for one project and identify who pays.
bands.11–12: Cost the reproducibility work for a real project, identify who pays, and put it in the real budget.

themes.description: Authorship criteria, applied honestly, including the conversation held before the work starts.

bands.K–2: Put every name on a group poster that did real work, and say what each person did.
bands.3–5: Agree before a group project who will be named and for what, and write it down.
bands.6–8: Apply a published authorship standard to a school group project and write the order down, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Apply a published authorship standard to a real project and write the order down.
bands.11–12: Apply a published authorship standard to a real project with the co-authors, before the work starts, and record the agreement.

themes.theme: Peer review as a service you owe
themes.description: Reviewing is a debt to a system that reviewed you, and it is done properly or not at all.

bands.K–2: Check a friend's experiment kindly and carefully, and tell them one thing to fix.
bands.3–5: Review a classmate's project write-up with a checklist and say what would make it better.
bands.6–8: Write one review of a school report to a standard you would be glad to receive, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Write one review to a standard you would be glad to receive.
bands.11–12: Write a real peer review for a real manuscript to that standard, and have the editor's or author's response confirm it was useful.

themes.theme: Explaining your work to a non-specialist
themes.description: Explaining your work without condescension and without losing the qualifications that matter.

bands.K–2: Explain your experiment to a younger child in one minute, then ask if they understood.
bands.3–5: Explain a school project to a family member in three minutes, and be corrected on one thing.
bands.6–8: Explain a school project in five minutes to somebody outside the subject, and be corrected.
bands.9–10: Explain your work in five minutes to somebody outside the field, and be corrected.
bands.11–12: Explain real research in five minutes to a real non-specialist audience, be corrected, and revise the explanation.

themes.theme: Dual use and thinking about it early
themes.description: Dual use considered at design time, when the design can still change.

bands.K–2: Say one good and one bad way somebody could use something you made.
bands.3–5: Write how a school invention could be used well and how it could be misused.
bands.6–8: Write the dual-use paragraph for a school project, honestly, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Write the dual-use paragraph for your own work, honestly.
bands.11–12: Write the dual-use assessment for real work at design time, and change the design where it warrants.

themes.theme: Funding and the influence it carries
themes.description: Where funding comes from, what it shapes, and what has to be declared.

bands.K–2: Say who paid for the things used in a class experiment and whether that changes anything.
bands.3–5: Find out who paid for a school science resource and whether that might shape what it says.
bands.6–8: Trace the funding of one paper and state what it could have influenced, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Trace the funding of one paper and state what it could have influenced.
bands.11–12: Trace the funding of a real body of work, state what it could have influenced, and write the disclosure that should accompany it.

themes.theme: Conflicts of interest in research, declared
themes.description: Declaring interests, including the ones that feel too small to mention.

bands.K–2: Say when judging a friend's experiment would be hard to do fairly.
bands.3–5: Write down anything that might make you unfair about a classmate's project.
bands.6–8: Write your own declaration of interests for a school project and have a classmate challenge its completeness.
bands.9–10: Write your own declaration and have somebody challenge its completeness.
bands.11–12: Write a real declaration of interests for a real submission, and have it challenged by a colleague and an office.

themes.description: Mentoring as a structured obligation rather than an ambient goodwill.

bands.K–2: Help a younger child with an experiment by asking questions instead of doing it for them.
bands.3–5: Agree with a younger student what help you will give them and when.
bands.6–8: Agree a written mentoring arrangement with a younger student, with expectations on both sides, checked by a teacher.
bands.9–10: Agree a written mentoring arrangement with expectations on both sides.
bands.11–12: Run a real mentoring arrangement for a term against written expectations and review it with the mentee.

themes.description: Leaving research without treating it as a failure, and what transfers.

bands.K–2: Say three things a scientist can do that are useful outside a laboratory.
bands.3–5: List three jobs a scientist's skills would fit outside research, and say why.
bands.6–8: Map a scientist's skills onto three non-academic roles, specifically, with a teacher checking.
bands.9–10: Map your research skills onto three non-academic roles, specifically.
bands.11–12: Map a real researcher's skills onto three real roles with somebody in each, and write the honest gap for each.

themes.description: Advising government: the difference between evidence and a recommendation, and who owns each.

bands.K–2: Tell the difference between what you found out and what you think people should do.
bands.3–5: Write what an experiment showed and, separately, what you would recommend.
bands.6–8: Write a one-page advice note for a school council that separates the evidence from the recommendation.
bands.9–10: Write a one-page advice note that separates the two explicitly.
bands.11–12: Write a real advice note for a real body that separates evidence from recommendation, and record how each part was used.

themes.theme: The public who paid for it
themes.description: Public money, public accountability, and what the public is actually owed.

bands.K–2: Explain your experiment to a visitor in words they would understand.

bands.11–12: Produce the plain-language summary for real publicly funded work, test it on the public, and publish it with the work.

themes.theme: Walking into a lab you do not know

themes.description: Structure that carries a claim, rather than a chronology of what you did.

themes.description: Writing the section that most determines whether the work is reproducible.

themes.description: What belongs in it, and the claim it must not exceed.

themes.description: Version control, ownership of sections, and the argument resolved before submission.

bands.9–10: Trace one real result to its use, or to its absence of use.
